title: SLOs, error budgets and Little's law
summary: Turn "fast and reliable" into numbers: SLIs, SLOs, error budgets and burn-rate alerts; then use Little's law and CPU time to work out concurrency and cores.

steps.title: SLI, SLO, SLA and the error budget
body: - **SLI** (service level indicator): a measured ratio of good events to all events, such as "requests answered with a non-5xx status in under 300 ms".
- **SLO** (service level objective): the target for an SLI over a window, such as "99.9% over 30 days".
- **SLA** (service level agreement): a contract with consequences (credits, refunds). Set it looser than the SLO.
- **Error budget**: what the SLO allows to fail. 99.9% means 0.1% may fail.
Time-based budgets for a 30-day window (43,200 minutes):
| SLO | Budget per 30 days | Per year (365 days) |
| 99.9% | 43.2 minutes | 8.8 hours |
| 99.95% | 21.6 minutes | 4.4 hours |
| 99.99% | 4.3 minutes | 53 minutes |
(You will also see "43.8 minutes" for 99.9%: that uses an average month of 30.44 days. Say which you use.)
The budget is a tool, not a punishment. While budget remains, ship features; when it is spent, spend the
time on reliability. Each extra nine costs roughly ten times more: 99.99% usually means several zones, automated
failover and no manual step in recovery, because 4 minutes is shorter than a human getting to a laptop.

steps.explain: 30 days are 43,200 minutes; 0.1% of that is 43.2 minutes. The rounding hides floating-point noise: `1 - 0.999` is not exactly `0.001` in binary.

steps.title: Burn rate: alert on how fast the budget goes
body: Alerting on "error rate above 0.1%" pages you for every blip. Alert on the **burn rate** instead:
```text
burn rate = observed error rate / error rate the SLO allows
SLO 99.9%  -> allowed 0.1%
1.44% errors for an hour -> burn rate 14.4 -> 14.4 / 720 hours = 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour
A common multiwindow setup for a 30-day 99.9% SLO (from the Google SRE workbook):
| Burn rate | Long window | Short window | Budget spent | Action |
| 14.4 | 1 hour | 5 minutes | 2% | page |
| 6 | 6 hours | 30 minutes | 5% | page |
| 1 | 3 days | 6 hours | 10% | ticket |
Both windows must be over the threshold: the long one proves it matters, the short one proves it is still
happening (so the alert clears soon after the fix).

prompt: **Alert.** A 99.9% / 30-day SLO. Over the last hour, 0.6% of requests failed; over the last 5 minutes,
0.7%. Using the table above, what should happen?
options: Nothing pages yet: the burn rate is about 6 over one hour, below 14.4. If it holds for 6 hours (with the 30-minute window also above 6) it pages
Page now: any error rate above 0.1% is an SLO breach
Page now: the burn rate is 60
Open a ticket: the 3-day window is certainly above 1
explain: 0.6% / 0.1% = burn rate 6. That is below the 1-hour page threshold of 14.4. The 6-hour rule catches it if
it continues. We cannot know the 3-day window from this. Paging on raw error rate is what makes on-call miserable.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The measured ratio of good events to all events
The internal target for that ratio over a window
A contract with customers, with penalties
The share of events allowed to fail
How many times faster than allowed the budget is being spent

steps.title: Little's law, and cores from CPU time
body: **Little's law** holds for any stable system: the number of requests inside it equals the arrival rate times
the time each one spends inside.
```text
L = lambda x W
2,000 requests/s x 0.25 s = 500 requests in flight
That is how you size thread pools, connection pools and concurrency limits: 500 in flight means a pool of
50 connections cannot work if every request holds one for the whole 250 ms.
The same idea gives **cores**. Each request uses some CPU time; a core gives 1,000 ms of CPU per second:
```text
cores = peak QPS x CPU ms per request / 1,000 / target utilisation
12,000 QPS x 10 ms / 1,000 = 120 cores busy; at a 70% target -> 172 cores
Why not plan for 100%? Because queues grow without bound near 100% (module 2 shows the curve), and you need
room for a lost server, a deploy and tomorrow's growth. Step through the numbers:

prompt: **Dashboard snapshot.** An API pool has 8 instances with 4 cores each. Peak traffic is 2,800 requests/s and
profiling says each request uses about 15 ms of CPU. p99 latency went from 80 ms to 6 s this morning and
keeps rising. What is going on?
options: Demand is 2,800 x 15 ms = 42 cores of work on 32 cores: the pool is past 100% and the queue grows every second
The pool is at 42% utilisation, so the problem must be the database
Little's law says 2,800 x 0.015 = 42 requests in flight, which is fine for 8 instances
p99 is always 75 times the median under load
explain: 42 cores of CPU work per second against 32 cores is 131% utilisation. Work arrives faster than it can be done,
so the queue (and latency) grows without limit. Add at least 6 instances to get under 70%: 42 / 0.7 = 60 cores = 15 instances.

steps.title: Error budgets and burn rate
prompt: Write two methods:
- `double ErrorBudgetMinutes(double slo, int days)`: the minutes the SLO allows to fail in a window of `days`.
`ErrorBudgetMinutes(0.999, 30)` is `43.2`.
- `double BurnRate(double errorRate, double slo)`: the observed error rate divided by the allowed one.
The tests round your results.
hints: A day has 24 x 60 minutes. The allowed failure share is `1 - slo`.

steps.title: Concurrency and cores
prompt: Write two methods:
- `double Concurrency(double qps, double latencyMs)`: requests in flight by Little's law.
`Concurrency(2000, 250)` is `500`.
- `int CoresNeeded(double qps, double cpuMsPerRequest, double targetUtil)`: the cores needed so the pool runs
at `targetUtil` (0 to 1), **rounded up** to a whole core. `CoresNeeded(12000, 10, 0.7)` is `172`.
starter: int CoresNeeded(double qps, double cpuMsPerRequest, double targetUtil)
solution: int CoresNeeded(double qps, double cpuMsPerRequest, double targetUtil)
hints: Latency is in milliseconds; Little's law wants seconds, so divide by 1,000.
Busy cores are `qps * cpuMs / 1000`. Divide by the target, then `Math.Ceiling` and cast to `int`.
template: Dojo.Eq("a fraction of a core still needs a core", 1, CoresNeeded(10, 1, 0.5));

steps.title: Build it: your first service
prompt: In the **System design board**, the parts of a small service are on the board but nothing is wired.
Wire **Users -> load balancer -> app servers -> database**, run the load test, and read the dashboard:
requests per second, p50/p95/p99 latency, utilisation of each part and the monthly cost. Meet the
availability and p99 goals the board shows.
steps.explain: Every later design is this one with more parts. Notice which part has the highest utilisation: that is where the next problem will come from.
